mechaber/1:main: 1. The Laws of Mourning on Chol Hamoed, 20 Seifim: One who buries a dead [relative] on a holiday does not have the obligations of mourning during the holiday. After the holiday, he observes shiva and mourns accordingly. He counts thirty days from the burial and observes the mourning practices for the remainder of the thirty days [that are after the holiday].
mechaber/2:main: 2. In places where they observe two days of Yom Tov, the shiva begins on the second day of the end of the festival, even if no mourning is observed then; because this day is only rabbinic, it counts towards the shiva, and one only counts six days following it. Rem"a: Regarding whether the second day of Rosh Hashanah counts towards the shiva, see glosses on Yoreh Deah 399:13.
mechaber/3:main: 3. One who buries his dead [relative] on the second day of yontif in the Diaspora that is the last day of the festival or the second day of Shavuot should observe mourning practices if that day is both the day of death and the day of burial. Because the second day of yontif is a rabbinic obligation and the first day of mourning is a Torah obligation, a rabbinic commandment can be superseded by a Torah commanded. However, if he was buried on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, we do not observe mourning practices because the two days are considered one long day. Rem"a: There are those who disagree and hold that one should not observe any mourning practices on the second day of yontif, and this is the widespread practice that should not be changed (Rabbeinu Hananel and the Rosh).
mechaber/4:main: 4. Regarding that which said that one who buries a dead [relative] on the holiday does not observe mourning practices, this is only referring to public practices. One does observe private practices. (However, it is permitted for the mourner to sleep in the same room as his wife, and no guard is needed [to ensure they do not have sex].)
mechaber/5:main: 5. Even though there is no mourning on a holiday, there is aninut [the first stage of mourning, prior to burial]. If somebody experiences a death on Chol Hamoed, the prohibitions applicable to aninut apply. If the person dies on Yom Tov and he does not wish to bury him that day, aninut is not applicable unless he goes to the edge of the techum to attend to the needs of burial immediately after the holiday, in which case aninut is applicable when it gets dark. However, if the death happens on the second day of Yom Tov and he wishes to bury him that day, or if it happens on the first day of Yom Tov and he wishes to bury him using non-Jewish labor, aninut applies.
mechaber/6:main: 6. Even though there is no mourning during the holiday, if somebody experiences a death on the holiday, we occupy ourselves with comforting him on the holiday. After the holiday, once seven days have passed since the dead, even though the mourning period has not finished, his work can be performed by others in their house and his servants can work in the privacy of his home. It is not necessary to comfort him the number of days that he was comforted on the holiday.
mechaber/7:main: 7. If the death occurred before the holiday and he observed mourning for even one hour before the holiday, shiva is no longer applicable and the days of the holiday count towards the thirty day [mourning period]. Thus, we consider there to be seven days before the holiday, we add the days of the holiday, and we add days after the holiday to complete the thirty day period. This is only applicable when one observed mourning in that hour. However, if one unintentionally or intentionally did not observe mourning practices, or it was close to nightfall and he was unable to observe, the holiday does not atrapalliate the need for mourning and the laws are the same as if the burial happened on the holiday.
mechaber/8:main: 8. If he observed seven days of shiva and then the holiday commenced, the thirty-day mourning period (shloshim) is nullified. Even if the seventh day of mourning is on the day before the holiday, he is permitted to get haircuts and do laundry on the day before the holiday. Rem"a: This is also the case for bathing for us who forbid bathing during shloshim; it is permitted to bathe close to the onset of the holiday and it is unnecessary to wait until night (Hagahot Maimoni, Mordechi, and Hagahot Ashiri). It is unnecessary to say that if the eighth day of mourning falls on Shabbat that is the day before the holiday, that is permitted to get haircuts on Friday. If he did not shave before the holiday, he is permitted to shave after the holiday, because shloshim has been nullified. However, he may not shave during the holiday, because it was possible for him to have shaved before the holiday. If the seventh day of mourning falls on Shabbat that is the day before the holiday, it is permissible for him to shave on hol hamoed because it was not possible for him to shave prior [to the holiday].
mechaber/9:main: 9. Regarding the holiday nullifying the shloshim period, this is only applicable to dead people that are not parents, for which it is forbidden to get a haircut until his friends scorn him. Even if the holiday occurs after the shloshim period, this practice is not nullified.
mechaber/10:main: 10. If a day of mourning that is not the seventh falls on the day before a holiday, it is permitted to do laundry, but he should not wear the clean clothes until night. It is good to be careful to do laundry after noon so that it is clear that he is doing laundry for the holiday. Bathing is forbidden until night. There those who permit bathing after the afternoon prayers, close to nightfall. Rem"a: For us, who forbid bathing the whole thirty-day period, it is forbidden to bathe [before the holiday], because the holiday nullified only the shiva [and not the shloshim]. The same is true for laundry in a place where the custom is to forbid laundry during shloshim.
mechaber/11:main: 11. Rosh Hashana and Yom Kipur are treated like festivals with respect to nullifying mourning.
mechaber/12:main: 12. If one practiced mourning for one hour before Passover, that hour counts as seven days. Together with the eight days of Passover, this is considered fifteen days. He adds another fifteen days [after Passover to complete the shloshim].
mechaber/13:main: 13. If one practiced mourning for one hour before Shavuot, that hour counts as seven days. Because if one did not sacrifice the Shavuot offerings on Shavuot, he can make it up for seven days, Shavuot counts as seven. Together, this is fourteen days. He adds another sixteen days [after Shavuot to complete the shloshim]. The second day of Shavuot counts towards the sixteen.
mechaber/14:main: 14. If one practiced mourning for one hour before Rosh Hashanah, the requirement for shiva is nullified because of Rosh Hashanah. Shloshim will be nullified by the onset of Yom Kippur. And he can shave on the eve of Yom Kippur. Similarly, if the burial was on the 3rd of Tishrei (so the 9th is the end of the Shiva), he can shave on the eve of Yom Kippur (which will nullify the Shloshim).
mechaber/15:main: 15. If one practiced mourning for one hour before Yom Kippur, the requirement for shiva is nullified because of Yom Kippur. Shloshim will be nullified by the onset of Sukkot. He can shave the day before sukkot.
mechaber/16:main: 16. If one practiced mourning for one hour before Sukkot, [the requirement for shiva is nullified because of Sukkot]. Together with the seven days of Sukkot, this is considered fourteen days. Shmini Atzeret is counted as seven days, which brings the total to twenty one days. Adding the second day of Shimi Atzeret brings the total to twenty two days. He adds eight more days [after the holiday to bring the total to thirty].
mechaber/17:main: 17. If one heard news of a relative's recent death on Shabbat or holiday, and by the end of the Shabbat or holiday it became distant news, the laws are the same as if one heard news of a non-recent death after the Shabbat or holiday. However, on Shabbat and yontif he should practice mourning practices privately.
mechaber/18:main: 18. If one heard distant news of a death on Shabbat or yontif, he doesn't even observe private mourning practices. After Shabbat or yontif, he practices one hour of mourning, and this is sufficient.
mechaber/19:main: 19. If one hears recent news of a relative's death on Shabbat, Shabbat counts as the first day. The following day he tears, and Friday will be the seventh day of mourning.
mechaber/20:main: 20. If ten days after Sukkot, he finds out that somebody died the day before Sukkot, even though if we were to count the hour before the holiday as seven, the seven days of Sukkot and Shimi Atzeret, together twenty one days, and the ten days afterwards, we would have thirty days, this is treated not as distant news but as recent news. The holiday does not count for one who did not practice any mourning prior to it; how much more so somebody who didn't even know about the death.

mishnah-berurah/10:ב: (ב) (h) It is permissible for the bass to be washed, but the hair is not allowed to be washed up on the day from the foot, but the hair is forbidden until the dark is taken:
mishnah-berurah/10:ג: (ג) Until midnight, he will not be held until the evening:
mishnah-berurah/10:ד: (ד) It is forbidden to bathe until night – even in the dunams, one can bathe at night in a cold garden and abroad, even in the palm of which seven are exalted:
mishnah-berurah/10:ה: (39) Some permit bathing, etc. — specifically bathing; but other mourning laws such as sitting on the ground and removing shoes apply until dark [Magen Avraham]:
mishnah-berurah/10:ו: (6) (m) Menacheh - means that it is necessary for him to pray a menechah first, then the sanctity of the foot applies to him [MA] and refer to the Yeshuat Ya'akov who wrote DMM while the day is long he practices the laws of mourning but close to darkness which is a bihash and it is possible to daf during the Tosaf Yot he does not practice and refer to the BH Siman Rasa wrote that the time for receiving Shabbat falls two hours close to evening:
mishnah-berurah/10:ז: (ז) (a) It is forbidden to bathe, etc. - R. near the darkness, and abroad should not be washed until the payment of our clothed as a haircut:
mishnah-berurah/10:ח: (42) For the festival is not nullified, etc. — nevertheless custom is lenient as Rama Yoreh De'ah 399:5; some later authorities hold one should not be lenient for hot bathing only cold [nevertheless on chol hamoed certainly rely to be lenient]; even per the lenient, hot bathing is only on erev Yom Tov and on chol hamoed because of festival honor; but after the festival bathing and laundering forbidden until thirty, for the festival did not nullify the thirty-day decree; see Hagahot Imrei Baruch Yoreh De'ah 399:
mishnah-berurah/13:_: (Mg) Oleg to the number of the 16th - after Dano in Kein in the regularity of Dircha and the main part of YoT is none other than Sunday:
mishnah-berurah/14:_: (44) Who shaves on Yom Kippur — for it is the seventh day and counts here and there; as above in seif 8; all the more permitted bathing and laundering; see below siman 426 — Magen Avraham end of siman sides regarding bathing one or two hours before dark and not before; in our case when seven are completed one may be lenient even before:
mishnah-berurah/15:_: (What) and shaving on the eve of the holiday - and when washing and washing are allowed up to 30 days, it is nothing but a ritual and the time of shaving and the rest is as explained in Sah Bahjah:
mishnah-berurah/16:א: (1) (Mo) And the eighth assembly of Sheba - that is a significant step in the P.E. and it takes seven days upon him, and even in Dashma himself he does not have to pay for his sacrifices like an assembly in the 33 mm since all the times are solemnized, they are all mutual.
mishnah-berurah/16:ב: (2) (Maz) And the second day of Shema, etc. - RL even abroad who do two days, Monday is considered thirty as the other days of the week so that it will not be necessary to add only eight more days:
mishnah-berurah/17:א: (1) (mh) He heard a close rumor - that is, that during L, his relative died:
mishnah-berurah/17:ב: (ב) His law is like the law, etc. — since he was unable to observe mourning at the time he heard, mourning did not apply to him at all.
mishnah-berurah/17:ג: (ג) (b) After the Shabbat and the foot, and not only one hour on the Shabbat and foot:
mishnah-berurah/18:_: It is a long way to say, that it is another day that you should take the oath
mishnah-berurah/19:_: (52) And the next day he tears — not literally; meaning motza'ei Shabbat. If he heard close report on Shabbat erev the festival, Shabbat counts for him one day and Yom Tov nullifies the seven-day decree [later authorities]; Pri Megadim Kaddish Yisrael wrote: the festival does not nullify and he has seven and thirty law even if he practiced one hour before the festival — see there:
mishnah-berurah/20:_: (Ng) that there is no rising habit, etc. - and from the mother of a woman who gave birth to a dead woman who must mourn for him, and the rest of the sick, and Aa for them to mourn because of their weakness, since they knew about it, but because of the rape, Aa for them to behave wretchedly, and the leg was hurt in the 7th, nullify from them the ruling of seven, and the 5a regarding the matter of thirty. The rest of the laws of the details pertaining to this matter are all explained in Yod Siman 46:
turei-zahav/2:_: This H. is interpreted in our words in the 4th, meaning that the 4th, we will only copy here a few revised laws where they are written in length and here in short: (a) Mena 17, 19, 20. This means that Efi was buried on the 1st according to Akoum, and not as the Rashel to divide strictly if he was buried on the 2nd, he is counted from the 2nd, but in the Rabbi's Ameri, if he was buried on the 2nd, the 7th is counted from the 2nd, but he was buried on the day A does not appoint Efi' from B's day 24th month of that in 3G:
turei-zahav/7:_: And festival days count for him toward the thirty — in Yoreh De'ah siman 399 Shulchan Aruch wrote: behold the law of thirty — namely laundering and haircutting — applies on the festival, and not only from festival law alone is it forbidden, but also from mourning law, for from festival law one may wear laundered new white garments, etc., and from mourning law it is forbidden in all of them; and this is Ramban's view. But Tur wrote, in the name of Rosh that even in mourning law it is permitted on the festival — what is permitted on the festival; and I wrote in Yoreh De'ah there one should rule like Ramban and not like Mishna Berurah who ruled like Rosh. Further I wrote there regarding a groom who married a woman on erev the festival and within the festival a relative died to him — he ruled in that book that although an ordinary groom for whom mourning occurred within the seven days of festivity does not count thirty except after the days of festivity, etc. — nevertheless this groom's days of festivity count toward thirty; and I wrote there this ruling is not correct, but here too they do not count for him, see there:
turei-zahav/10:_: to wash etc. In the B.D. C. Shachat S.A. B.S.A. and Rama, we have the permissive practice of bathing after the offering prayer close to darkness, and this [contradicts] the MS here. And the Eik' as a mash in the 14th and there I wrote to justify his words:
turei-zahav/16:_: And the holiday after all It is true that when a person died before the leg, I reckoned that he died on the foot or in the house.
turei-zahav/19:_: And this is the 7th day of Lavilot. In the Gemara, I wrote a davmat of the 7th day on Shabbat, and now, on the 7th day of the Shabbat, it is permissible to practice a prohibition according to my words, that she worshiped only at dawn, in the hot bird, and in the Menach, it happened to S. Della, as the psalmist, in this I also wrote there, "If on the 7th day of Shabbat, it is customary for the owners of houses to sit on the land for one hour at night, it is a complete mistake, but Heard a distant rumor on Shabbat that then he practices mourning for one hour at night and not like the late Rabbi in this:
